1317.title: Chevra Kadisha: True Kindness
1317.hook: volunteers who prepare the body for burial
1317.carry: kindness to the dead is true kindness
1317.howItsDone: Jewish communities may have a chevra kadisha, a burial society of volunteers who prepare the body for burial, with women caring for women and men for men; some also arrange the shemira and help the family with the funeral.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shomer, the one in the chair through the night, and your line was the dead are honored, never left alone. Today, the people who come in the morning.
screen: `THE DEAD ARE HONORED, NEVER LEFT ALONE.`

segments.voice: "Deal kindly and truly with me." Jacob says it near the end of Genesis, old and dying in Egypt, to his son Joseph. His request is specific: don't bury me here. Carry me home, and lay me with my fathers. Joseph swears he will. Notice what Jacob asks for. Not money, not a blessing. A burial done right, by someone he trusts, after he can no longer say thank you. Jewish communities built a whole institution around that request.
screen: `DEAL KINDLY AND TRULY WITH ME.` → `BURY ME WITH MY FATHERS.` → `HE CAN NEVER SAY THANK YOU.`

segments.voice: It's called the chevra kadisha. Chevra means a society, a group of companions; kadisha is Aramaic for holy. The holy society prepares a body for burial: washing it, dressing it, placing it in the coffin. They are usually volunteers, ordinary people, a teacher, a dentist, a retired bus driver, who answer the phone when someone dies. Women care for women and men for men. You met Jacob's words in your first year. The commentator Rashi, reading them, says kindness done for the dead is true kindness, chesed shel emet, because the one receiving it can never repay. No thanks, no favor returned, no one to impress. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses dies on a mountain, and the text says he was buried there, and that no one knows his grave. The rabbis read it as God himself burying Moses. So, they teach, as God buries the dead, so should you. The holy society does what the tradition calls divine work, with rubber gloves and a basin. Some societies keep a yearly day of their own, linked to the memory of Moses, with a fast and then a meal together. The rest of the year, the work is quiet. A society is holy not because of who joins, but because of what it does for people who can't ask.
screen: `VOLUNTEERS WHO ANSWER THE PHONE.` · `TRUE KINDNESS: NO REPAYMENT.` · `GOD BURIED MOSES.` · `HOLY BECAUSE OF THE WORK.` · then, large: `CHEVRA KADISHA: TRUE KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind people who do work few people see: hospice volunteers, night-shift nurses, whoever washed the dishes at the last funeral you went to. Picture one of their faces and thank them silently, by name if you know it. If you pray, you can pray for them.
Chevra kadisha. The holy society: volunteers who prepare the dead for burial, doing true kindness that can never be repaid. Today's word.
Your line: kindness to the dead is true kindness. It can never be repaid. That's today, done.

1318.title: Washing and shrouds
1318.hook: the body is washed and dressed in plain white shrouds, the same for everyone
1318.howItsDone: Before a traditional Jewish burial, members of the chevra kadisha perform tahara, washing the body with care and pouring water over it, then dress it in simple white shrouds called tachrichim; some men are also wrapped in their tallit.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chevra kadisha, and your line was the holy society: true kindness that can't be repaid. Today, what the holy society actually does.

Families were running away from their own dead. That's the scene the Talmud describes. Burial had become so expensive, with fine clothes and costly display, that for some, the cost of a funeral was harder to bear than the death itself. Some relatives would leave the body and flee. Then Rabban Gamliel, a leader of his generation, made a request about his own funeral: bury me in plain linen. The people followed him, and carried out their own dead in linen too.
screen: `FAMILIES FLED THEIR DEAD.` → `BURY ME IN PLAIN LINEN.` → `THE PEOPLE FOLLOWED.`

segments.voice: Before that plain linen comes tahara, purification: the ritual washing of the body, done by the holy society. The body is cleaned gently and thoroughly, the face kept covered and only the part being washed uncovered, out of modesty. Then water is poured over the whole body in a continuous flow. Members say verses and prayers as they work, and in some communities, at the end, they say: tehorah hi, she is pure, or tahor hu, he is pure. Then the shrouds, called tachrichim: plain white garments, usually linen or cotton, sewn by hand, with no pockets, and in some traditions no buttons or knots. A Yiddish saying goes: shrouds have no pockets. You take nothing with you. A rabbi and a cab driver, a philanthropist and a person who died with nothing: dressed alike. That goes back to Rabban Gamliel. Equality in death wasn't an accident; it was a decision, made so no family would be shamed. Some men are also wrapped in their own tallit, the prayer shawl, with one fringe cut. In the book of Job, after losing everything, Job says: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither." Tahara treats the body almost as a newborn is treated: washed by others, wrapped by others, held by others.

segments.voice: Look at what you're wearing, and notice what in it says something about you: a brand, a ring, a badge, a style. Without judging any of it, ask: if all of this were replaced with one plain white garment, what would still be me? If you pray, you can say the line from Job slowly, or sit in silence.

1319.title: Plain wood, soon
1319.hook: burial comes quickly, often in a plain wooden coffin
1319.howItsDone: Traditional Jewish burial takes place soon after death, with short delays allowed for the honor of the deceased, such as for close relatives to arrive; the coffin is usually plain unfinished wood, and in some places the body is buried in shrouds without a coffin.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tahara, the washing, and your line was everyone equal in death. Today, the box and the clock.

A showroom at a funeral home. Polished mahogany with brass rails, a quilted satin lining, a model with a name like a luxury car. And in the corner, almost apologetic, a simple box of unfinished pine. A family sits down with a salesman, still in shock, the phone buzzing with relatives booking flights. For Jewish families who keep the tradition, two decisions are made before they walk in. The box will be the plain one. And the funeral will be soon.
screen: `MAHOGANY AND BRASS.` → `A PINE BOX IN THE CORNER.` → `TWO DECISIONS ALREADY MADE.`

segments.voice: The plain coffin follows from yesterday: everyone equal in death, and no family made to feel it has to spend to show love. Traditional coffins are simple wood, unpolished, and some are made without metal at all, joined with wooden pegs. Then the earth. After Eden, God tells Adam, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." A plain wooden box lets that happen. It doesn't try to hold back the earth; it lets the body go home. In some places, Jews are buried in shrouds alone, with no coffin at all. Then the clock. The Torah, speaking about someone executed and hung up, says the body must not stay up overnight but be buried that same day. The rabbis drew a wider principle: leaving the dead unburied is a disgrace, so bury promptly. That's why a Jewish funeral can come so fast, sometimes within a day. And the exception. Waiting can serve the dead person's honor too. The Talmud allows a delay for the sake of the dead, to bring a coffin or shrouds, and later codes add time for close relatives to arrive. What isn't allowed is delay for its own sake. The rule and the exception point the same way: what honors this person? Both are about the person in the box, not the people looking at it.
screen: `NO ONE SPENDS TO SHOW LOVE.` · `DUST TO DUST.` · `BURY THE SAME DAY.` · `WAIT ONLY FOR THEIR HONOR.` · then, large: `PLAIN WOOD.`

segments.voice: Find one plain thing near you made of wood, cloth or stone, a table, a chair, a doorframe, and rest your eyes or your hand on it. Notice how it asks for no attention and still does its job every day, then ask where, in your own life, plain would do. If you pray, you can hold the line about dust in your mind, or sit in silence.
Plain wood. A simple coffin, the same for everyone, letting the body return to the earth, and a burial that comes soon, for the honor of the dead. Today's word.
Your line: plain wood. Simple honors the dead better than show. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1320.title: Keriah: The Mourner's Tear
1320.hook: mourners tear a garment or a ribbon
1320.carry: mourners tear their clothes, and bless the true judge
1320.howItsDone: Before a Jewish funeral, close mourners perform keriah, tearing an outer garment or a black ribbon while standing and saying the blessing 'blessed is the true Judge' (baruch dayan ha-emet); the torn garment or ribbon is worn during the days of mourning.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was plain wood: a simple coffin, and burial soon. Today, a sound mourners make before a single word is spoken.

His sons bring him a coat, torn and stained with blood, and ask him to identify it. Jacob knows it at once: Joseph's. He believes his favorite son has been killed by a wild animal. Genesis doesn't give him a speech. It gives him an act. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Jacob rent his garments." He tore his own clothes. Jewish mourners still do the same in the minutes before a funeral, sometimes with the help of a rabbi holding a small blade.
screen: `A TORN COAT.` → `JACOB TEARS HIS GARMENTS.` → `BEFORE THE FUNERAL.`

segments.voice: Keriah means tearing, and it's old. Jacob tears his clothes over Joseph. David tears his when news comes that Saul and Jonathan have fallen. Job, hearing that his children have died, stands up and tears his robe; you met his friends sitting silent beside him in your third year. Grief in the Bible isn't only felt; it's done with the hands. The mourner stands, the way Job stood up, and the rabbis learned from his verse that the tear is made standing: you meet grief upright. The tear is on the outer garment, a shirt, a jacket, a blouse. In some communities the tradition is to tear on the left side, over the heart, for a parent, and on the right for other close relatives. Some mourners instead tear a black ribbon pinned to their clothes, so the garment itself is spared. As they tear, mourners say an old blessing: blessed is the true Judge. It's hard to say. It doesn't pretend to understand. In the worst moment, it still names God. Why tear at all? A loss can rip something open inside a person, and polite clothes can hide it. Keriah lets the outside match the inside. Through the days of mourning, the torn garment is worn, a visible sign that says: something is missing, don't expect me to be fine. No explanation needed.
screen: `JACOB, DAVID, JOB.` · `MADE STANDING, OVER THE HEART.` · `BLESSED IS THE TRUE JUDGE.` · `THE OUTSIDE MATCHES THE INSIDE.` · then, large: `KERIAH: THE MOURNER'S TEAR.`

segments.voice: Let one loss come to mind, a death, or a friendship, a place, a life that didn't happen, and name it quietly without explaining it. Place a hand over the left side of your chest, where the tear would go, and let the loss be real for a few breaths without hurrying to feel better; if you pray, you can say the old words, blessed is the true Judge. If grief ever feels like too much to carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
Keriah. Tearing: a garment or ribbon torn standing, over the heart for a parent, with the words blessed is the true Judge. Today's word.
Your line: mourners tear their clothes, and bless the true Judge. Jacob tore his over Joseph. Until next time.

1321.title: The funeral
1321.hook: eulogy, psalms, and the prayer "God full of mercy"
1321.howItsDone: A Jewish funeral is usually simple: a eulogy (hesped), psalms, and the memorial prayer El Male Rachamim, sung by a cantor or rabbi with the name of the person who died; it is often sung again at the graveside.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was keriah, and your line was the tear: grief made visible. Today the mourners, torn garments and all, walk into the funeral.

No flowers on the plain wooden coffin. Folding chairs, a small chapel, people in coats they don't wear often. A grandson unfolds a sheet of paper and tells a story about fishing that makes the whole room laugh, then go quiet. Someone reads a psalm. Then the cantor, or a rabbi, or a friend who knows the tune, begins to sing in Hebrew, slow, rising and falling, and in the middle of it comes a name: the name of the person in the coffin, sung out loud. Today's word is that song.
screen: `A PLAIN COFFIN, NO FLOWERS.` → `A STORY ABOUT FISHING.` → `A NAME, SUNG OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: It's El Male Rachamim, God full of mercy. But first the eulogy, the hesped, which you met in your first year with Abraham. When Sarah dies, Genesis says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her." The rabbis saw a eulogy there. A hesped is meant to do both: speak about the person, and let people weep. The codes ask the speaker to praise truly, not to invent a saint, because an honest picture honors the dead more than a flattering one. Psalms are read, and Psalm twenty-three may be among them: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." It's read as company for the road, not as an explanation. Then the prayer. El Male Rachamim is a short memorial prayer, usually sung. It calls on God full of mercy, who dwells on high, to give true rest to the soul of the one who has died, beneath the wings of the divine presence, and it names them. It asks that their soul be bound up in the bond of life. It may be sung again at the grave, and later on days of remembrance. In the middle of that slow melody, one ordinary name is sung as if it belongs there. The funeral says out loud, together, that this person mattered, and hands them, by name, to mercy.

1322.title: Isaac and Ishmael at One Grave
1322.hook: mourners shovel earth into the grave themselves
1322.carry: filling the grave is the kindness of truth
1322.howItsDone: At a Jewish burial, after the prayers, mourners and friends take turns placing earth into the grave themselves; in some communities the shovel is put back into the earth rather than handed from person to person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the funeral, and El Male Rachamim. Your line: god full of mercy. Today, the graveside, a little longer.

"And Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him." That's how Genesis, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, closes the story of Abraham. Two brothers who grew up apart, one sent away into the wilderness as a boy, stand at the same grave. The text doesn't say they made peace. It says they buried their father. Once the prayers are said, the shovel doesn't stay with the cemetery workers. The daughter picks it up. Then the brother. Then the old friend from work. Earth lands on a plain wooden lid, slow and heavy and hard to watch. The tradition calls it a kindness.
screen: `ISAAC AND ISHMAEL AT ONE GRAVE.` → `THE MOURNERS TAKE THE SHOVEL.` → `EARTH ON PLAIN WOOD.`

segments.voice: First, the sons at the grave. Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham. A generation later, Genesis says the same of Isaac: his sons Esau and Jacob bury him, two more brothers with a hard history. Whatever lay between them, the burial was theirs to do. Second, the name. Earlier this week you met Rashi's phrase for care of the dead: chesed shel emet, the kindness of truth, a kindness the one who receives it can never repay. Filling the grave is its last act, and the tradition gives it to the people who loved the person, not only to strangers. It makes the death real. Nobody leaves the cemetery thinking it was a dream. Third, the small customs. In some communities the first scoops are taken with the back of the blade, so it doesn't look like ordinary digging. And nobody hands the shovel over. You push it back into the mound and step away, and the next person picks it up on their own. Some explain the back of the shovel as reluctance, and putting it down as not handing grief from one person to the next. Communities give different reasons, and keep the custom anyway. Fourth, the circle. Friends and neighbors take a turn too, because the work is shared. The person in the grave will never know who lifted the earth. No one is left to say thank you, and the shovel goes round anyway.
screen: `BROTHERS AT ONE GRAVE.` · `THE KINDNESS OF TRUTH.` · `NOT HANDED, PUT DOWN.` · `NO ONE LEFT TO THANK YOU.` · then, large: `ISAAC AND ISHMAEL AT ONE GRAVE.`

And if the grief you're carrying is your own and it feels like too much, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

1323.title: Seven days
1323.hook: mourners stay home seven days; visitors bring food and sit with them
1323.howItsDone: After a Jewish funeral, the closest mourners stay home for shiva, sitting low; friends and neighbors bring meals, visit, and often gather so the mourners can say Kaddish at home, and visitors traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shovel at the graveside. Your line: the last kindness. Today the mourners go home, and the door stays open.

What do you say to someone whose mother was buried this morning? The book of Job has a strange answer. Job has lost his children, his wealth, his health. Three friends travel to him. When they see him, they weep and tear their clothes. Then, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, they sit with him on the ground "seven days and seven nights", and nobody says a word, because they can see how great his grief is. Some readers say it's the best thing those friends do in the whole book.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU SAY?` → `JOB'S FRIENDS ARRIVE.` → `SEVEN DAYS ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Shiva means seven. You first met Job's silent friends back in year three; today, the week itself. First, the seven days. When Joseph buries his father Jacob, Genesis says "he made a mourning for his father seven days." Jewish mourning keeps that week. After the funeral the closest family stay home and sit low, on low chairs or cushions. In some homes mirrors are covered. Work stops, and the world comes to them. Second, the silence. The Talmud learns from Job's friends that comforters don't speak first. You come in, sit, and wait for the mourner to open. If they want to talk about the person who died, you listen. If they want silence, you give it. You don't have to find the right sentence; the tradition takes that job away from you. Third, the food. The mourners don't cook the first meal after the burial; neighbors and friends bring it. All week people keep arriving with soup and bread and trays nobody asked for, and in some homes a group gathers each day so the mourners can say Kaddish without leaving the house. Leaving, visitors say a traditional line asking that God comfort the mourners among all who mourn for Zion and Jerusalem. Fourth, the week just past: the holy society, the washing and the shroud, plain wood, the tear, God full of mercy, the shovel, and now seven days of company. Step by step, the dead are honored, and then the living are not left alone.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS AND SEVEN NIGHTS.` · `WAIT FOR THE MOURNER TO SPEAK.` · `OTHERS COOK THE FIRST MEAL.` · `THE WEEK, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `SIT WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Picture someone who is grieving, now or not long ago, and yourself sitting near them, low, saying nothing: no advice, no sentence about better places or reasons, only your company. Let the quiet be the gift, and if you pray, hold them in your prayer. And if the grief is your own and it feels like too much, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
Shiva. Seven: the week the mourners stay home, and the world brings food and sits with them. Today's word.
Your line: sit with them. Your company says what no sentence can. See you tomorrow.
